name: View Down Frederick Street to St Stephen's and the Kingdom of Fife
address: Frederick Street at George Street, Edinburgh
description: From this point at the top of Frederick Street, the New Town's dead-straight grid opens onto one of Edinburgh's most celebrated views: the street runs directly downhill for half a mile, closing on the tower of St Stephen's Church in Stockbridge before the view carries on past it, across the Firth of Forth, to the hills of Fife beyond. William Playfair designed St Stephen's, built in 1827-28, specifically to terminate this vista - its tower rising 162 feet to dominate the skyline exactly where Frederick Street, Howe Street and St Vincent Street all converge below.
interesting_fact: St Stephen's clock, fitted by James Ritchie & Son in 1828, carries the longest pendulum of any public clock in Europe - 60 feet long, swinging with an 8.6-second period inside the tower. The far shore on a clear day is Fife, still known traditionally as "the Kingdom of Fife" from its days as a distinct Pictish territory rather than part of mainland Scotland proper. St Stephen's stopped holding regular Church of Scotland services decades ago and became Saint Stephen's Theatre; in 2026 the building itself went up for sale, its spire still framing the same view Playfair intended two centuries earlier.

name: Hard Rock Cafe
description: Behind the neon sign sits a Georgian townhouse dating from George Street's original 1780s development as one of the New Town's grand residential streets. By 1882 the building had become Dowell's Rooms, a well-known Edinburgh auction house, before a later spell as a public house. Hard Rock Cafe took over the premises in 1998, adding its trademark gold guitar logo to a facade that had already lived through a century of very different Edinburgh trades - a pattern repeated up and down George Street, where grand Georgian frontages now house everything from banks to bars behind their original stonework.
interesting_fact: The "Love All, Serve All" motto worked into the doorway lettering here is the same one displayed at every Hard Rock Cafe worldwide, dating back to the very first branch, opened in London in 1971 by two young Americans, Isaac Tigrett and Peter Morton, who wanted an American-style diner that welcomed absolutely everyone. That founding philosophy of inclusivity is also why Hard Rock cafes fill their walls with rock memorabilia rather than velvet ropes; Edinburgh's own collection has included Ringo Starr's leather jacket and a guitar once played by Red Hot Chili Peppers.

name: The Standing Order
description: This grand banking hall, all soaring columns and coffered ceiling, was built in 1874-78 as the Edinburgh headquarters of the Union Bank of Scotland, designed by the noted Scottish architect David Bryce and completed after his death by his nephew John Bryce. Grade A listed, it's one of George Street's most imposing former banks - a street that was lined with them in the Victorian era - and Wetherspoon converted it into a pub while keeping much of the original interior intact, including the vast scale and detailing that once signalled a bank's solidity and trustworthiness to its customers.
interesting_fact: The pub takes its name, "The Standing Order", from banking terminology as a nod to the building's past - and that past is still visible throughout. One of the dining areas contains an original Chubb vault, its markings inside dated 1968, while a bronze statue nicknamed "Money, Money, Money" - a bank manager offering up a case of cash - watches over the main hall, a wry piece of commentary on the building's former trade planted right in the middle of what's now one of Scotland's best-regarded Wetherspoon pubs.

name: Thistle Street Bar
description: This snug traditional pub occupies a building put up around 1775-80 on Thistle Street, often reckoned the oldest street laid out in Edinburgh's New Town - a narrow service lane running parallel to George Street, originally intended for tradesmen's workshops and stables rather than grand frontages. True to that humble origin, the building itself started out as a cow shed before its later life as licensed premises; today it's known for a proper cask-ale selection from independent Scottish breweries and regular live folk music sessions.
interesting_fact: In the late 1970s and early 1980s the pub traded as Marr's Bar, named for its then-landlord Archie Marr - who had previously played drums as one of the earliest members of the Bay City Rollers, the Edinburgh pop group who became one of the biggest-selling acts in the world during their mid-1970s "Rollermania" peak, with tartan-clad fans queuing for hours at record-shop signings. The band's own name is said to have been picked at random by throwing a dart at a map of North America, which happened to land near Bay City, Michigan - a detail that's stuck with the group's story ever since, even though the lineup itself, including Marr, changed repeatedly through the band's early years.

name: Fishers in the City
description: Fishers in the City occupies a converted warehouse on Thistle Street, opened in 2001 as the second branch of a Leith seafood institution that's been family-run since 1991. The menu leans hard into the classics - chowder, fishcakes, fish and chips, and a rotating shellfish selection - alongside meat and vegetarian dishes given equal attention, served in a warm, contemporary dining room built for long, unhurried lunches as much as celebratory dinners.
interesting_fact: The original Fishers restaurant still operates a few miles away on the historic waterfront at The Shore in Leith, inside a striking round stone tower built in 1685-86 by the architect Robert Mylne as a windmill, later stripped of its sails and topped with battlements in 1805 to serve as a harbour watchtower. This Thistle Street branch doesn't share that landmark building - its own premises are a plainer former warehouse - but the family recipes and seafood sourcing carry over directly. Now in its third generation of family ownership, Fishers has grown from that single Leith address, opened in 1991, into one of Edinburgh's most consistently well-regarded seafood groups.

name: Cafe Marlayne
description: This intimate French bistro on Thistle Street opened its doors on 27 February 2000, founded by Islay Fraser and Marcelline Levicky, who blended their two names to create "Marlayne". The menu draws its inspiration from the bistros and brasseries of Marcelline's hometown, Lyon, reworked with the best Scottish produce available - classic French cooking served with the kind of care and precision that's kept the small, lively room busy for a lunch crowd by day and a more romantic dinner trade after dark.
interesting_fact: Cafe Marlayne became successful enough to open a second branch on Old Fishmarket Close, just off the Royal Mile - a location that's since moved again, now trading at the top of Leith Walk, while this original Thistle Street bistro remains the flagship. More than two decades after opening, it's still independently and personally run by its founders rather than having expanded into a wider chain, something diners and reviewers regularly point to as central to its lasting appeal.

name: The Merchants' Hall
description: The Merchants' Hall is the headquarters of the Company of Merchants of the City of Edinburgh, a body whose roots trace back to the trade guilds of the 13th and 14th centuries, formalised into its modern form by a Royal Charter granted by Charles II in 1681. The current 19th-century building on Hanover Street, a Category B listed structure, was built to project exactly the values the Company still associates itself with - integrity, commercial acumen and civic accomplishment - and its interior includes a genuinely striking Minstrels' Gallery. The Company's influence reaches well beyond this one hall: it still founded and funds two of Edinburgh's best-known independent schools, George Watson's College and Erskine Stewart's Melville, continuing a charitable and educational role that stretches back through the Company's entire 340-plus-year history.
interesting_fact: The Hall runs a permanent exhibition inside chronicling the Company's full history 'from 1681 to the present day' - meaning this working private hall, still used for events and private hire, is also one of Edinburgh's more discreet, lesser-known small museums.

name: Former TSB Bank, Hanover Street
description: This imposing neo-Greek bank building, a Category A listed structure, was built in 1939 to designs by the architects Oldrieve, Bell and Paterson for the Edinburgh Savings Bank, later absorbed into the TSB network whose name still sits carved above its entrance. Its tetrastyle Ionic portico - four full-height fluted columns across the Hanover Street facade - is built from Darney sandstone on a plinth of light grey Creetown granite, with the substructure masonry by G. and R. Cousin of Edinburgh and the superstructure by Jackson, Brown of Giffnock. Decorative roundels above the flanking entrances carry TSB's own arms, a two-towered castle with a closed portcullis, while the arms of Edinburgh, Leith and Musselburgh appear elsewhere on the facade, marking out the three burghs the bank originally served.
interesting_fact: The building's banking hall was designed on a genuinely double-height scale, built in 1939 to project total financial permanence and trustworthiness right as the Second World War was breaking out - and the site has since been earmarked for conversion into a pub and restaurant, a change of use that will keep the grand banking hall but end its 85-plus years as a working bank.

name: All Bar One, George Street
description: This grand Georgian corner building at the junction of George Street and Hanover Street was originally constructed as a bank, its scale and formal stone facade - with balustraded upper storeys and heavy classical detailing wrapping both street frontages - built specifically to project financial solidity on one of the New Town's most prominent corners. Like many of Edinburgh's historic bank buildings, it has since been repurposed for hospitality; it now trades as an All Bar One, with the original double-height banking hall giving the modern bar an unusually grand, high-ceilinged interior far larger than a purpose-built pub of the same footprint would ever have.
interesting_fact: The building's position - directly on the crossing of George Street and Hanover Street, two of the New Town's principal axes - meant that whichever bank originally built it was making a deliberate statement of prestige simply through its address, long before anyone had heard of All Bar One.
